title: From Retrieval to Reasoning: Building Production-Ready Agentic AI Systems with Knowledge Graphs
gist: RelationalAI's Cassie Shum reports that her own A/B experiment killed her prior thesis: with today's models, a knowledge graph no longer improves accuracy over dumping ~30 documents into context — correctness was identical — but it sharply cuts tokens and agent turns, so the case for graphs moves from accuracy to efficiency, provenance and visibility. She also publicly reverses her earlier 'code is cheap, spec is the real truth' position, arguing the implementation, not the spec, is the source of truth.

themes.theme: The experiment that reversed the accuracy thesis

insights.claim: In a controlled experiment running the same on-call policy task twice — once with a knowledge graph and once by feeding the agent all roughly 30 documents — the correctness of the resulting implementation was identical in both instances, contradicting the hypothesis that graph retrieval improves accuracy.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Accuracy-based sales pitches for graph retrieval are now falsifiable and failing; vendors must reprice on efficiency instead.
insights.quote: What happened was nothing. The correctness of actually the implementation I was trying to do was actually right in both instances. Guess what? Models are really good.
insights.locator: Essentially, what we ran as an experiment

insights.claim: The measurable difference from using a knowledge graph was in tokens consumed and the number of turns the agent took before reaching the right answer, not in the quality of the answer.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Turns-to-answer becomes the operative KPI for agent infrastructure — directly convertible into inference cost savings.
insights.quote: The number of turns. How often did that agent wander before getting to the right answer? I think that's incredibly important now.
insights.locator: It's about how quickly you can actually turn around

insights.claim: Token inefficiency compounds with headcount: an implementation pattern multiplied across 10,000 engineers turns wasteful context-stuffing into a material cost line.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Enterprise agent economics are governed by per-task token efficiency at scale, not per-query accuracy — a budget argument, not a quality one.
insights.quote: Take this implementation and take it times 10,000 engineers. Those tokens are going to add up if you just keep feeding it all the documentation in the world and say, go figure it out.
insights.locator: Take this implementation and take it times 10,000 engineers

insights.claim: Developer productivity measurement should shift from how many tokens a developer uses to how efficiently they use agents and how many turns an agent takes to reach the target.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Argues against token-consumption metrics that AI coding vendors currently report — a measurement standard still up for grabs.
insights.quote: That goes against that token thing of like how many tokens are a developer using. It should be, how efficient are you using the agents, really?
insights.locator: That goes against that token thing

insights.claim: The speaker saw a clear retrieval differentiator for graphs as recently as six months prior but no longer does, because model capability erased it — an unusually fast obsolescence of an architectural advantage.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Model progress is destroying scaffolding-layer moats on a six-month clock — a direct risk to retrieval-tooling valuations.
insights.quote: I would say, maybe even six months ago, I saw the differentiator in actually retrieving from a graph.
insights.locator: Is GraphRAG Dead?

insights.claim: The experiment was run at roughly 30 documents, and the untested question is whether accuracy advantages reappear and turn savings widen at the scale of thousands of documents in a customer environment.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: The null result may be scale-limited — the real test of graph value is enterprise-scale corpora, still unproven.
insights.locator: With that back there was 30 docs

themes.theme: Why a knowledge graph rather than long context

insights.claim: Long context can produce good logic in a single window, but the unsolved problems are repeatability, consistency and accountability when every person on a team writes a different prompt.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Variance across prompts — not model quality — is the enterprise blocker; shared context stores are the proposed fix.
insights.locator: Why the Knowledge Graph (KG) is the Foundation

insights.claim: A knowledge graph's primary organisational value is as a shared, composable source of context across a team or company, allowing time-travel queries into what was known and how relationships formed.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Positions graphs as a governance and consistency layer, a different buyer and budget than search/retrieval tooling.
insights.locator: For me, one of the biggest things of a knowledge graph

insights.claim: The defensible asset in AI is not the model but the domain knowledge and the graph built from it, because models change constantly and can be fine-tuned by anyone.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Classic 'data is the moat' argument, restated for the agent era — favours incumbents with proprietary operational data.
insights.quote: the moat isn't really the models. The models are changing constantly. You can fine-tune your models. There are different domain models.
insights.locator: One of the things that I think about

insights.claim: Questions like which compliance regime applies, what Tier 1 means, or what was decided last quarter have specific answers inside a financial institution that a general-purpose agent cannot produce, because the answer is organisational context rather than domain knowledge.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Defines the exact query class where enterprise context stores beat frontier models — compliance and internal-policy questions.
insights.locator: Here are some questions that were asked in one of these financial institutions

insights.claim: Domain and organisational context change over time, so decisions made today under current technology and rules may differ from those made six months or five years ago, and that lineage of decisions must itself be tracked.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Temporal versioning of institutional knowledge is an underbuilt product category distinct from static document search.
insights.locator: it's really about how domain and context changes over time

insights.claim: Agents do not know what to do with tribal knowledge, because half of it lives in engineers' and analysts' heads and the rest sits in stale Confluence and wiki pages with no indication of which rules are still live.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Pointing agents at existing enterprise wikis actively injects stale rules — a hidden failure mode in 'connect your docs' AI deployments.
insights.quote: Agents don't know what to do with tribal knowledge. Half the tribal knowledge is in all of our engineers and business analysts' heads, and the other half of it is in old Confluence pages or wiki pages
insights.locator: Then, I also say things around like veterans, tickets, internal wikis

insights.claim: Graphs are a way to bind multiple domains and expose cross-domain dependencies, which matters where microservice teams have drifted into a distributed monolith with untracked dependencies.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Dependency discovery across services is a concrete, measurable use case for graph adoption in large engineering orgs.
insights.locator: What happens if you have dependencies on all of these different domains

themes.theme: Agents as a mirror of engineering culture

insights.claim: Agents are not magic; they are a fast, honest mirror of an organisation's engineering culture, shoring up missing fundamentals and amplifying whatever practices already exist.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Predicts AI productivity gains will be highly dispersed across companies based on pre-existing engineering maturity, not on tool choice.
insights.quote: agents aren't really magic, they are just the fast, honest mirror of your engineering culture
insights.locator: Really, what I've found out is agents aren't really magic

insights.claim: Agents collapse the feedback loop on a bad or empty spec from two to four weeks under scrum to roughly 40 minutes, which is an opportunity only if teams are equipped to act on it.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: A ~100x compression in requirements feedback latency reshapes product process more than it reshapes coding throughput.
insights.locator: Now we're in this world where agents are actually accelerating

insights.claim: Spinning up many agents let the team push features very quickly, but the speaker was unsure how useful those shipped things actually were — velocity rose without a matching signal on value.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Warns that agent-driven output metrics decouple from outcomes — a caution for any 'AI productivity' due diligence.
insights.quote: we were pushing a lot of things, but I'm not sure like how useful these things were
insights.locator: when we first started out working with all of these agentic technologies

insights.claim: A startup whose founders vibe-coded an entire application in three months demoed successfully to an excited customer, then fell apart on production scalability because testing practices and CI/CD were never in place.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Concrete pattern for diligence: AI-built demos can pass customer review while carrying zero production readiness.
insights.locator: My partner just joined a startup

insights.claim: Bad engineering cultures with undefined rules, brittle handoffs and inconsistent data will very quickly produce poor code once agents are introduced, while good cultures ship correctly and fast.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Agent adoption widens the gap between well- and poorly-run engineering organisations rather than levelling it.
insights.locator: these good engineering cultures, like a task that's actually created here

insights.claim: Rather than retrieval as a query, context should be assembled as a bundle combining the spec, the engineering standards, prior work and relevant documentation before the agent starts.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Context assembly, not retrieval, is the emergent design pattern — a different product shape from vector search.
insights.locator: Pattern 1 - Context Assembly

insights.claim: Asked to implement authentication and authorization, an unaided agent will go to the internet and copy how Stripe or Facebook did it, whereas binding the organisation's existing GitHub repos and a current architecture document into the context produces the organisation's own pattern.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Default agent behaviour imports external architectural conventions into regulated codebases — a concrete governance risk.
insights.locator: Pattern 1 - Context Assembly

insights.claim: Storing policy documents in a graph lets a team ask which documents are in its own neighbourhood — which of several teams' on-call policies actually apply — a disambiguation neither a human nor an agent can do reliably from a flat document pile.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Nearest-neighbour scoping of policy is the specific mechanism behind the token savings, and is hard to replicate with flat RAG.
insights.locator: One of the things that I did was, in this experiment

insights.claim: Provenance should start at idea creation by a human, not when an agent picks up the task, so the audit trail spans the full path from idea through spec, task pickup, implementation and production.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Defines the audit boundary regulators will eventually demand for AI-written software — most tooling starts too late.
insights.quote: That provenance starts much earlier on, not right when you actually picked up the task.
insights.locator: Pattern 2 - Provenance for Decision Making

insights.claim: Human interventions in an agent's work should themselves be captured as first-class provenance data, recording how many times a human had to step in and what feedback they gave.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Human-intervention counts are a measurable proxy for agent reliability — a metric AI vendors currently do not expose.
insights.locator: One of the things that we've built in our harness

insights.claim: Each status-timeline action is written to the knowledge graph and summarised, creating a flywheel where every decision feeds back into the same graph that supplies context for the next task.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: The compounding-context flywheel is the mechanism by which an internal graph could become a real switching cost.
insights.locator: Every time something happened on a status timeline

themes.theme: Pattern 3 — code is truth, spec is a kernel

insights.claim: The speaker publicly reverses her own position from six months earlier that code is cheap and the spec is the real truth, concluding instead that the spec captures intent while the code is what is real.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts the spec-driven-development thesis that has attracted AI tooling investment over the past year.
insights.quote: I was recorded on a podcast saying, "Code is cheap, spec is the real truth." I said that six months ago.
insights.locator: Pattern 3 - Reliability Under Exploration

insights.claim: Regenerating the spec on each agent pass was a concrete mistake because the agents erased what the builder discovered during implementation; the fix was to summarise the actual implementation and write that back.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Spec regeneration is a silent knowledge-destruction bug in spec-driven agent workflows — a design defect to check for in tooling.
insights.quote: the agents erased what the builder discovered
insights.locator: One of the things that we got wrong

insights.claim: The implementation consistently knows more than the plan, so a knowledge graph must model both intent (spec) and reality (code) and reconcile them in a loop.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Bidirectional spec/code reconciliation is a product gap that current AI coding tools largely do not fill.
insights.quote: The implementation definitely knew way more than the plan did.
insights.locator: The implementation definitely knew way more

insights.claim: Treating an agent as fire-and-forget — hand it a spec and walk away — does not work, because it produces no flywheel and does not end with what was wanted.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Fully autonomous delegation remains unviable in practice, capping near-term labour-substitution claims for coding agents.
insights.locator: The other thing that we found out is treating the agent as a fire and forget

insights.claim: Assuming inference engines are interchangeable was mostly but not entirely correct; the unsolved part is carrying forward accumulated context and corrected patterns into the next feature.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Model portability is high but context portability is not — context stores, not models, create lock-in.
insights.locator: The other thing was we were assuming that the engines were interchangeable

insights.claim: The most basic missing capability was visibility into what agents are actually doing — which tasks they are on, how many tokens they use, and what context bundles they started from.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Fleet-level agent visibility is an unbuilt category that teams are hand-rolling — a clear tooling opportunity.
insights.quote: What on God's green earth are our agents doing?
insights.locator: Pattern 4 - Visibility

insights.claim: Because everything was stored in the graph, the team could later query cost per task, how many tasks shipped in a period, context bundle size and full audit trails without instrumenting separately.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Per-feature token cost becomes a reportable engineering metric — a new line item for CFOs evaluating AI spend.
insights.locator: It's like, that's why we held everything in the graph

insights.claim: The harness demonstrated was built internally by a small group of the speaker's own developers rather than being a product, indicating the tooling layer for agent governance is still being improvised in-house.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Widespread internal building of the same harness is the classic precondition for a commercial category to form.
insights.quote: that's just a bunch of devs clamoring something together
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: Knowledge graphs carry substantial overhead and should only be used where the benefit is visible; the speaker explicitly advises caution because the cost of building one is still high.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: A graph vendor's own VP warning about build cost is a meaningful caveat on the addressable market for graph infrastructure.
insights.quote: The knowledge graph definitely has a lot more overhead. My advice is only use it when you see that benefit.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: Building a knowledge graph requires domain expertise and organisational context, and the speaker's company is now using agents themselves to build knowledge graphs faster in order to compress the zero-to-working effort.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Agents lowering the cost of graph construction is the plausible path to graph adoption at scale — watch that unlock.
insights.locator: We're using agents right now to figure out how to build that knowledge graph

insights.claim: The knowledge graph should be the context layer itself rather than a component sitting beneath the agent, though the speaker concedes this is a biased view and pragmatically it sits alongside other document context.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Context engineering is consolidating into a named architectural layer, and whoever owns it owns the agent stack's memory.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: Graph query performance depends on the data volume being traversed and on how the graph was constructed, with no simple rule — a large graph can become a performance issue while small traversals will not.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Unquantified scaling behaviour is an open technical risk in graph-backed agent architectures.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: The unresolved problems the speaker names are how to manage and supervise agents, when to use a graph versus other approaches, and how to build an agentic memory architecture at scale on top of the four patterns.
insights.speaker: Cassie Shum
insights.so_what: Names the three gaps where the next generation of agent-infrastructure products will be built.
insights.locator: Open Questions: What's Still Open?
